fact: Bengal tigers have striped skin, not just striped fur — the pattern is unique to each individual, like a fingerprint. India holds roughly 70% of the world's wild tiger population.
Asian elephants, found across central and southern India, are one of the few animals known to mourn their dead, sometimes standing vigil over a deceased herd member's remains for days.
The Asiatic lion survives in the wild only in Gir Forest, Gujarat — the last population of this subspecies anywhere outside Africa.
India reintroduced cheetahs in 2022 at Kuno National Park, over 70 years after the species was declared extinct in the country — the world's first intercontinental large-carnivore translocation.
The Indian peacock, India's national bird, can't actually fly far — its train feathers are too heavy for sustained flight, so it relies mostly on running and short bursts to escape predators.

Greater flamingos flock by the thousands to the Rann of Kutch in Gujarat, one of the largest flamingo breeding grounds in Asia; their pink color comes entirely from pigments in the shrimp and algae they eat.
The great Indian one-horned rhinoceros, concentrated in Assam's Kaziranga National Park, has skin so thick and armor-like it looks like natural plating — yet it's soft enough to be prone to sunburn.
House crows, common across Indian cities, can recognize individual human faces and hold grudges against people who've wronged them, passing that recognition on to other crows.
The sloth bear, found across the Indian subcontinent, uses its long lower lip and gap-toothed mouth like a vacuum to noisily suck up termites and ants.
Sarus cranes, the tallest flying birds in the world, mate for life and are revered in Indian folklore as a symbol of marital devotion.
